patches.origin: treebank; upstream owns the tree-sitter-bash name on crates.io, so the redistribution publishes under its own: package name, repository, homepage and description. [lib] name stays tree_sitter_bash so the crate is a drop-in replacement. include gains LOCAL-PATCHES.md, ledger.json and patches/* so provenance travels inside the published tarball. patches.title: case patterns with more than three concatenated parts
patches.origin: treebank; found by the top-500 Debian sweep

evidence.diagnosis: _extglob_blob allowed exactly `extglob_pattern`, or `extglob_pattern` + one of string/expansion/command_substitution + one optional trailing extglob_pattern. A case pattern with more parts than that had no path at all. autoconf writes five-part patterns in every configure it generates — `*"\n"enable_$ac_useropt"\n"*`, which is extglob + string + word + expansion + string + extglob — so this rejected 392 of the corpus's 344 configure scripts and their siblings. The fix makes the tail a repeat over the same set plus word, raw_string and simple_expansion; the shape of the tree (repeated `value` fields) is unchanged, because _extglob_blob already produced more than one.
evidence.evidence_note: 367 files, zero regressions: noise_files stayed at 148 across the change and all 100 upstream corpus tests still pass. On the GitHub corpus this patch fixes NOTHING (1434 gaps before and after), which is the sharpest single piece of evidence that the two artifact populations are different languages in practice.
evidence.upstream_status: not reported upstream yet; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

patches.title: substring expansion with a variable offset
patches.origin: treebank; found by both the Debian and the GitHub sweep

evidence.diagnosis: _expansion_max_length lists what may appear in the two `:` positions of a substring expansion. The SECOND position already had `optional($.simple_expansion)`, so `${a:1:$n}` parsed; the first did not, so `${a:$off:1}` and `${a:$off}` had no path. One line, and it makes the two positions symmetric.
evidence.evidence_note: The one patch here that both corpora wanted: 16 files on Debian and 41 on GitHub, where array slicing with a computed offset is ordinary modern bash.
evidence.upstream_status: not reported upstream yet; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

patches.title: for loop with no word list
patches.origin: treebank; found by the top-500 Debian sweep

evidence.diagnosis: for_statement required a $._terminator between the variable and the do_group. bash requires one only when there IS a word list: `for i do ... done` is valid (the `do` delimits by itself) and `for i in a b do ... done` is not. The terminator moved inside the `in` branch, with an optional one on the branch without it, so `for i; do`, `for i<newline>do` and `for i in a b; do` are untouched and `for i in a b do` is still rejected — verified explicitly, because widening a rule that also feeds `select` is exactly where an accepts-invalid regression would hide.
evidence.evidence_note: 38 files on Debian, 5 on GitHub — POSIX-sh idiom, so it lives where the shell has to run under dash as well as bash.
evidence.upstream_status: not reported upstream yet; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

patches.title: = is a synonym for == in a test command
patches.origin: treebank; found by the GitHub sweep

evidence.diagnosis: binary_expression offered the glob-pattern right-hand side ($._extglob_blob) to `==` and `!=` only. bash treats `=` as a synonym for `==` in a test command, so `[ "$arg" = -- ]` had no path at all. The new branch sits at PREC.ASSIGN rather than joining the `==`/`!=` one at PREC.EQUALITY, because `=` already occupies ASSIGN in the operator table and one operator cannot hold two precedences — tree-sitter reports that as an unresolvable conflict on `[ x || y = z ]`. SCOPE, STATED: this reaches single-bracket `[ … ]` only. Inside `[[ … ]]` the dedicated _test_command_binary_expression rule routes `=` to the external _regex_no_space token, which the LEXER resolves before the parser can pick this branch, so `[[ $x = *"a b"* ]]` is still rejected. Offering _extglob_blob there too was tried: it generates cleanly, needs a [$.binary_expression, $._test_command_binary_expression] conflict, and changes nothing at all, because the scanner has already decided. That is a scanner fix and was not attempted blind.
evidence.evidence_note: 12 files on GitHub, 0 on Debian, zero regressions — noise stayed at 592 and 148 and all 103 upstream corpus tests still pass. Small, and stated as measured: the large `[[ ]]` half of this construct is the part the scanner still owns.
evidence.upstream_status: not reported upstream yet; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

patches.title: herestring after another redirect
patches.origin: treebank; found by the GitHub sweep

evidence.diagnosis: redirected_statement's redirect list was repeat1(choice(file_redirect, heredoc_redirect)) — no herestring. A command with an inline herestring parses through `command`, but once a file_redirect has pulled the command into a redirected_statement the herestring has nowhere left to attach. The herestring hangs off the END of that repeat1 rather than joining it, and that placement is the whole patch: joining the repeat also matches a LONE herestring, which re-shapes `node <<< foo` from an inline child of `command` into a redirected_statement wrapper — a tree-shape change consumers' queries would feel, and upstream's own Herestrings corpus test catches it. Measured: the joined version failed that test, the appended version passes all 103.
evidence.evidence_note: 142 files on GitHub and 5 on Debian, zero regressions: noise stayed at 592 and 148. The largest single patch in this grammar after 0003.
evidence.upstream_status: not reported upstream yet; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

patches.title: arithmetic operands built by concatenation
patches.origin: treebank; found by the top-500 Debian sweep

evidence.diagnosis: The arithmetic rules had no notion of concatenation at all: _arithmetic_literal listed number, subscript, expansions, variable names and strings as ALTERNATIVES, so a literal glued to an expansion had no path. bash expands an arithmetic operand to text first and reads it as a number only afterwards, so `0x` + a command substitution is ordinary and gnupg2's autogen.sh uses it to turn `git describe` output into a revision number. The new hidden rule takes a number or variable name followed by one or more expansions or command substitutions, aliased to the existing `concatenation` node so the tree shape is one consumers already know.
evidence.evidence_note: 22 files on Debian and 13 on GitHub, zero regressions: noise stayed at 148 and 592, and the c-style `for ((i=0;i<3;i++))` header and ordinary `$((a + b * 2))` were regression-tested explicitly, since this rule feeds both.
evidence.upstream_status: not reported upstream yet; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

generate_cli_note: same pin as the other grammars: tree-sitter-cli 0.26.x ships broken Unicode identifier tables (see treebank-rust ledger). Noted for this grammar in particular: upstream's committed src/parser.c is byte-identical to what 0.25.10 generates, so materialization changes no generated file until a patch does.

oracle.tool: `bash -n` via lang::exec_oracle, the shared fork-per-file driver
oracle.note: Values restructured from this ledger's own corpus.oracle / oracle_version / oracle_version_note by the treebank-lua change that made this field mandatory; no fact here is new. bash's own parser, which reads the whole script and executes nothing; TWO-VALUED. The shell's version fixes the DIALECT as well as the language version: this is the reference parser for the sh/bash/dash files admit() admits and for nothing else, and pointing it at zsh, ksh, fish or csh would turn the grammar's correct rejection of another language into a reported gap. Reject statuses are [1, 2] and are measured, not anticipated — see corpus.oracle_reject_statuses; 126 and 127 stay outside that list on purpose, so a mistyped corpus root fails loudly instead of marking every file invalid.

corpus.source: Debian sid source packages (.orig.tar.*, upstream's own release archive, not the distro-patched tree), ranked by popcon installs per SOURCE package. Bash is the first language here with no package registry at all, so the corpus has to come from artifacts. Two artifact sources are implemented and BOTH are measured, because they are different populations: lang/debian.rs (default) and lang/github.rs, selected by TREEBANK_BASH_CORPUS.
corpus.ranking: popcon (popularity-contest) install counts. It counts machines rather than dependency edges, which makes it the same KIND of metric as crates.io/npm/PyPI downloads rather than Java's dependent-repos proxy.
corpus.ranking_note: SHELL IS A GUEST LANGUAGE. No package is written in shell; it arrives as build glue, init scripts, test harnesses and maintainer helpers inside packages written in something else — the largest bodies of shell in sid belong to git (278k lines, mostly its test suite), systemd (41k) and bash itself (8.9k next to 135k of C). So the filter cannot be C's 'more of this than of that'; it is a floor, sh >= 500 lines anywhere in the package. Measured over the 1061 packages the walk looked up: 87% contain some shell, 61% have >= 100 lines, 48% >= 500, 38% >= 2000. The threshold is therefore not very selective, and that is the honest picture — shell is nearly everywhere. The consequence to state: popcon installs are attributed to the PACKAGE, not to its shell, so this ranks 'shell that ships inside software people install', which is not the same thing as 'popular shell scripts'.
corpus.size_cap: 250 MB per artifact (Lang::max_artifact_bytes). Registry tarballs are bounded by what an author publishes; artifacts are not. The top 500 Debian sources by popcon come to 11.5 GB, of which 7.6 GB is EIGHT packages — texlive-extra (3.2 GB), chromium, qt6-webengine, texlive-lang, texlive-base, firefox-esr, libreoffice, qtwebengine — 1.6% of the corpus for two thirds of the bytes. All eight are skipped and logged by name. This is a real change to the population: chromium and firefox-esr carry tens of thousands of lines of shell each and are NOT in these numbers.
corpus.files_note: Shell is also the first language here whose files mostly have NO EXTENSION. Measured on this machine's /usr and /etc, 933 of the 963 shell scripts present are found by shebang and only 124 by *.sh/*.bash — an extension-only rule would have seen 13% of them. classify() therefore takes the extensions and names tree-sitter.json claims (.sh, .bash, .ebuild, .eclass, .bashrc, .bash_profile) PLUS every extensionless file as a candidate, and admit() decides the candidates on their first line, using upstream's own first-line-regex (^#!.*\b(sh|bash|dash)\b.*$) as an ALLOWLIST. It has to be an allowlist: an extensionless file is a candidate precisely because its name says nothing, so perl, python, awk and expect must be denied admission rather than merely not-denied. Files containing a NUL byte are dropped (bash refuses them outright). Files that are TEMPLATES rendering to shell are excluded too — see template_filter.
corpus.composition_note: What 'shell Debian ships' actually means, measured: of 25,663 files and 498 MB, 344 are autotools `configure` (200 MB, 40% of the bytes) and the next six most common filenames are install-sh, build.sh, missing, depcomp, compile and ltmain.sh — generated autotools and libtool boilerplate, near-identical across packages. 12% of the corpus files are byte-for-byte duplicates of another file in it. They are kept rather than filtered because they are real, and the most widely distributed shell in existence, but a gap count from this corpus must be read with the clustering: ONE autoconf bug is 392 gap files (see patch 0003).
corpus.oracle: `bash -n` via lang::exec_oracle, the shared fork-per-file driver — bash's own parser, which reads the whole script and executes nothing. TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. See ORACLE.md for the full write-up; that it does not execute was verified with live canaries before any corpus file was fetched, and 'source /absent/file is not an error' is only one of eight probes.
corpus.oracle_version_note: The shell's version IS the language version and is load-bearing exactly as generate_cli is. It also fixes the dialect: this is the reference parser for the sh/bash/dash files admit() admits and for nothing else. Pointing it at zsh, ksh, fish or csh would turn the grammar's correct rejection of another language into a reported gap.
corpus.oracle_cost: 2.4 s per 1000 files serial, of which 83% is process startup (0.7 ms bare spawn, 1.6 ms bash startup, 2.0 ms on an empty file, 2.4 ms on real files ~6 KB each — so only ~0.4 ms is parsing). The ROADMAP recorded 3.6; both figures are mostly a measurement of fork+exec on their own hardware and the part that belongs to bash agrees. bash cannot syntax-check a file from inside a long-lived shell (set -n stops that shell executing the `source` that would read the next file), so it is a fork-per-file oracle like `php -l` and inherits exec_oracle rather than reimplementing it: measured through the sweep over 2205 files, 7.30 s at one worker against 2.25 s at sixteen, i.e. the oracle itself goes from ~5.3 s to ~0.25 s — 0.11 s per 1000.
corpus.oracle_honesty: 963 real shell scripts from this machine's /usr and /etc: 952 valid, 11 invalid, ZERO false rejects. All 11 were read and are genuinely not bash — ten netpbm `#!/bin/sh` polyglots whose bodies are Perl, and one ucf documentation example whose `: if test ...; then` really is a syntax error.
corpus.oracle_limits: bash's parser defers everything that is not syntax, so `$(( 1 + + ))` and `${!}` are VALID here and fail at runtime, and an unterminated heredoc is a warning. Correct for a parse-only oracle — the grammar treats those regions as text too — but it means this oracle can never be evidence for TIGHTENING the grammar inside arithmetic or expansions.
corpus.fetched: Debian sid index 2026-08-11; corpora re-extracted 2026-08-12 when the template filter landed (GitHub repos re-pinned to that day's HEADs)
corpus.packages_note: 500 requested; 492 fetched. The 8 missing are exactly the size-cap skips listed under size_cap.

github_corpus.what: The same sweep against the other artifact source: 492 of the top 500 repositories GitHub's linguist calls Shell, ranked by stars, pinned at a commit sha. TREEBANK_BASH_CORPUS=github; corpus/bash-github/.
github_corpus.bytes_note: 163 MB across 41,923 files — mean 3.9 KB, against Debian's 19.4 KB. GitHub shell is many small scripts; Debian shell is a few enormous generated ones.
github_corpus.finding: THE TWO POPULATIONS DISAGREE, and the patch series is the proof rather than the assertion. Over the whole series the split is even (Debian 942 -> 494, GitHub 1010 -> 778), but no single patch helps both equally: 0003 fixed 392 Debian files and ZERO GitHub ones because it is an autoconf construct; 0007 fixed 142 GitHub files and 5 Debian ones because a herestring after a redirect is modern hand-written bash; 0006 fixed 12 GitHub and 0 Debian. A corpus of one population would have found perhaps half of these.
github_corpus.ranking_bias: Stars are attention, not use: the weakest popularity metric in this repo, and it does not decay. `language:Shell` is linguist's majority vote over a repository, which put ohmyzsh (zsh), d3 (JavaScript) and papers-we-love (a reading list) in the top ten. Gap files are also concentrated — 839 of 1,388 come from three repositories — where Debian's spread across 492 independently-maintained sources.
github_corpus.template_contamination: RESOLVED by the template filter; see corpus.template_filter. Before it, 419 of 1,388 GitHub gap files (30%) were Jinja templates that `bash -n` called valid. The number now excludes them at corpus-build time rather than carrying a caveat.
github_corpus.drift_note: A GitHub repository has no version, so `resolve()` pins whatever HEAD was at fetch time and a re-fetch moves the corpus. Between the 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-12 fetches several repositories advanced (community-scripts/ProxmoxVE 962dbbb -> 4bf3fda, ComplianceAsCode/content 0e64629 -> 86d9ab4). The before/after pair above was therefore re-measured on the SAME post-filter corpus, upstream grammar and patched, rather than compared across fetches. The filter's own effect was predicted on the pre-filter corpus at 678 files / 445 gaps and observed at 646 / 443, so drift accounts for little of it, but the honest way to state a GitHub sweep is with the fetch date attached.

corpus.remaining_gaps_note: 522 Debian gap files remain, in three groups. (1) 107 autotools `configure` files still fail, at a whole-file ERROR whose first-error signature is line 1, so the report cannot point at the construct; delta reduction over a 12,248-line prefix did not converge inside a 20-minute budget and it is not diagnosed. Not guessed at. (2) 60 files, `x=1 >/dev/null` — a single variable assignment followed by a redirection and no command name, which bash runs as a command whose only lasting effect is the assignment (libtool's ltmain.sh probes shell features with `__PLUSEQ_TEST+=" b" 2>/dev/null`). TWO OR MORE assignments already parse, through variable_assignments; exactly one does not, because `command` consumes the assignment as a prefix and then demands a name. Attempted and reverted: adding the no-name alternative to `command` generates cleanly once `[$.command]` is declared internally ambiguous, and it fixes the herestring form (`x=1 <<< hi`) but not the file_redirect form, which `redirected_statement`'s prec.dynamic(-1) still wins. A correct fix needs that precedence interaction worked out rather than a bigger hammer. (3) The tail: 19 files of `$((0x$(...)))`, 13 of `) fi`, and ~200 singleton clusters.
corpus.over_acceptance_note: The negative corpus is 14 files, not 18. FOUR candidates were rejected by bash and ACCEPTED by the grammar, so they cannot be committed as negative tests without failing verify.sh, and they are recorded here instead because they are the accepts-invalid-code direction GRAMMARS.md warns about: (1) `f() { }` and every other empty compound body — bash requires at least one command in `{ }`, `( )`, `do ... done` and `then ... fi`, and the grammar makes all of them optional (`case x in esac` is the one bash really does allow, and the grammar is right there); (2) a stray `done`, (3) a stray `esac`, and (4) `: if test -d /x; then` — all three the same root cause, which is that the grammar lets a reserved word be an ordinary command_name where bash treats it as a syntax error in command position. Both are upstream's, both are real, and neither was patched here: (1) is a one-token change per rule but a tightening, which needs its own before/after sweep to show it breaks nothing, and (2)-(4) need the reserved-word set threaded through the external scanner.
corpus.oracle_reject_statuses: [1, 2], and the 1 is measured rather than anticipated. `bash -n` exits 2 for a syntax error nearly everywhere and 1 when the error is inside an ARRAY-ASSIGNMENT WORD LIST: `x=( a+([0-9]) )` exits 1 where `echo a+([0-9])` and `case $y in a+([0-9])) ;; esac` exit 2. Exactly one file in the 67,586 across both corpora does this — linux's tools/testing/selftests/wireguard/netns.sh — and with only 2 in the list it would abort the whole sweep. 126 (bash refuses a binary or a directory) and 127 (no such file) stay OUTSIDE the list on purpose: if every non-zero status meant invalid, a mistyped corpus root would score every file invalid, gap_files would fall to zero and the sweep would report a flawless grammar. admit() scans the whole file for a NUL, not a leading window, so a 126 cannot reach the oracle; no admitted file in either corpus contains one.
corpus.template_filter:
A file carrying a Jinja/Django STATEMENT tag — `{% if … %}`, `{%- from … %}`, and the `{{% … %}}` delimiters ComplianceAsCode configures — is a template that renders to a shell script, not a shell script, and admit() drops it. This is the one filter here that exists because of an ORACLE limit rather than a corpus one: `bash -n` calls those files VALID, since the tags happen to lex as shell words, so they arrive as grammar GAPS rather than as noise. No two-valued per-file oracle can tell the difference.

Anchored on a keyword, not on `{%`, and that was measured rather than assumed. A bare `{%…%}` rule matched 10 Debian files of which EIGHT were false positives: `{%s%}` in gettext's OCaml format-string fixtures, `{%%k1%}` in libgcrypt's and grub2's configure, `{% %%}` in gitk. All are valid shell. Interpolation alone is a worse discriminator still — `{{ … }}` matches 1,818 GitHub files of which only 461 fail, because `docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Image}}'` is ordinary shell — so it is deliberately NOT filtered on. `comment` is left out of the keyword list because ceph ships a shell script that emits a Jekyll post containing `{% comment %}`.

Measured effect: Debian loses ONE file (a ceph bootstrap script that really is a template, `/mnt/{{ ceph_dev_folder }}/src/…`, 13 tags), gaps 522 -> 521. GitHub loses 646 files, gaps 1,388 -> 945 and noise 817 -> 592. Residual: 31 GitHub gap files still carry a bare `{{ }}`, and sampled they are docker/kubectl Go-template format strings — real shell, correctly kept — plus 7 ComplianceAsCode files with no statement tag. Zero gap files in either corpus still carry a statement tag.
corpus.patch_evidence_note: The per-patch sweep_before/sweep_after numbers below were measured on the PRE-TEMPLATE-FILTER Debian corpus of 25,663 files (943 gaps down to 522). The filter later removed one file from it, and that file was a gap, so every patch-level figure is one lower against the current 25,662-file corpus. Left as measured rather than silently restated.
